feed.title: PHP October 2026: what's new
feed.subtitle: PHP news for October 2026, led by the month's big story: two critical security flaws in PHP (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, nicknamed php2shell). The current situation in plain words, the core facts with their evidence, what to do, and a briefing for every kind of reader.

entry.summary: every section versioned and every fact given a timeline: each briefing, front-page section and story page records the release that wrote it, with its history and a diff of every change; a page per fact, from publication to this site; what's new, release by release, with a feed; the fact pipeline; the editor interviewed in his own words; a sitemap, robots.txt and structured data for search engines From the editor: what's new must be visible, every section must say which release wrote it, a version must move only when what its reader sees changes, and every fact needs a timeline.

entry.title: v0.3.1: the site is renamed PHP October 2026, PHP news for the month rather than one nickname, and its front page is now jargon-free and about the c
entry.summary: the site is renamed PHP October 2026, PHP news for the month rather than one nickname, and its front page is now jargon-free and about the current situation: right now, at a glance, the core facts each with its status and evidence, what nobody knows yet and the latest; the technical front page moved to the specialist summary From the editor: the site should be named for PHP in October, not for the incident, so that it can carry whatever PHP news the month brings; and the first page must be readable by anyone.

entry.summary: the first reader-first pass: fifteen named readers mapped by job and technical depth, a briefing for each opening with a thirty-second plain answer and a reading path, three new briefings (curious reader, website owner, project manager), a plain-English explainer, a glossary of 40 terms linked and hover-defined on first use on every page, every CVE ID linked, a plain-English line on every technical page, a reader bar that keeps your place, and a front page that leads with where things stand and who you are Designed from the question the editor asked: who is reading, and what does the first screen do for them?
